unit.title_en: Small talk: weather and the weekend
unit.can_do_en: talk about the weather and say what I did.

brief.situation_en: Maria asks her neighbour Leena about the weather.

lines.speaker: Maria
lines.text_kirja: Hei Leena! Tiedätkö sinä, sataako huomenna?
lines.gloss_en: Hi Leena! Do you know if it's going to rain tomorrow?

judge.reason: Same greeting and question about whether it will rain tomorrow; only register differs.

lines.speaker: Leena
lines.gloss_en: It shouldn't. Tomorrow will be sunny.

judge.reason: 'Ei pitäs' is the spoken form of 'Ei pitäisi'; the rest is identical.

lines.speaker: Maria
lines.gloss_en: Good! I want to go to the beach.

judge.reason: Mä haluun and minä haluan are the same: I want to go to the beach.

lines.speaker: Leena
lines.text_puhe: Hyvä idea. Tänään oli tosi tuulista.
lines.text_kirja: Hyvä idea. Tänään oli todella tuulista.
lines.gloss_en: Good idea. It was really windy today.

judge.reason: 'Tosi' and 'todella' both mean 'really'; the meaning is identical.
Joo/kyllä are both 'yes'; mun/minun sateenvarjoni is 'my umbrella'. Same meaning.

lines.speaker: Leena
lines.text_puhe: Voi ei! Mä voin lainata sulle mun vanhan sateenvarjon.
lines.text_kirja: Voi ei! Minä voin lainata sinulle minun vanhan sateenvarjoni.
lines.gloss_en: Oh no! I can lend you my old one.

judge.reason: Same offer to lend my old umbrella to you; only pronoun forms differ in register.
Kiitti is spoken for kiitos; tosi equals todella. Same meaning.
"Nähään" is just the spoken form of "nähdään"; both mean "see you tomorrow" and the rest of the line is identical.

forms.why_en: Moi is the everyday spoken hello. Books and formal texts write hei.

forms.form_name_en: present tense, 2nd person singular, with the question ending -ko/-kö
forms.why_en: In Tiiätsä, speech says tiiät for tiedät and joins sä. Books write tiedätkö sinä.
Means 'you' (one person). Spoken: 'sä'.

forms.form_name_en: present tense, 3rd person singular, with the question ending -ko/-kö
forms.why_en: sataa, to rain, with the question ending -ko: sataako? Speech uses -ks: sataaks.
This is the dictionary form. People say it the same way.
Ei on its own answers 'no'. Speech says it the same way.

forms.lemma_meaning_en: to have to, to like, to hold
forms.why_en: Pitää with -isi for 'should': pitäisi. Speech shortens it to pitäs.
Means 'is': present tense, 3rd person singular, going with 'Helsinki'.
The partitive after on for weather: on aurinkoista.
Means 'good!' or 'great!', showing you are happy.
Means 'I'. Spoken Finnish often says 'mä'.
Haluta with -n for 'I': haluan. Speech says haluun.
This is the dictionary form. People say it the same way.
Ranta with -lle for 'to', and nt turns to nn: rannalle.
This is the dictionary form. People say it the same way.
This is the dictionary form. People say it the same way.
Olla, to be, in the past tense for he, she or it: oli.
Books write todella. In speech people use tosi, 'really', instead.
tuulinen, windy, becomes tuulista after 'oli' when talking about the weather in general.
Yes. In everyday speech people often say joo instead.
Minä with -n: minun pitää means I have to. Speech shortens it to mun.

forms.form_name_en: nominative singular, with the possessive ending for my
forms.why_en: Books add -ni for 'my': sateenvarjoni. Speech drops it and says mun sateenvarjo.
Mennä, to go, in the past tense for he, she or it: meni.
This is the dictionary form. People say it the same way.
This is the dictionary form. People say it the same way.
Voida, can, with -n for 'I': voin.
This is the dictionary form. People say it the same way.
Sinä with -lle for 'to, for'. Speech shortens it to sulle.
Vanha with -n to match the umbrella after lainata: vanhan.

forms.form_name_en: nominative singular, with the possessive ending for my
forms.why_en: Books add -ni for 'my'. Speech says mun and adds -n instead: mun sateenvarjon.
Thank you, said by the customer; in casual speech it becomes kiitti.
Means 'nice'; 'Kiva tavata' = 'Nice to meet you'.

forms.meaning_en: you're welcome (literally: it does not last)
forms.why_en: Ei kestä is the polite reply to thanks. After ei the verb drops its ending: kestää becomes kestä.
The passive form means 'let's see each other'. Speech drops the d: nähään.
